vuln_id: SEC-bench mruby.ossfuzz-42532953 / memsearch_swar stale post-memchr bounds check

classification.classification_note: The reproduced fault is an out-of-bounds heap read in `memsearch_swar()` when the fallback substring scan calls `memcmp()` after `memchr()` has moved the candidate pointer near the end of the haystack but the guard still checks the stale pre-`memchr` span length.

bug_description.original: Heap-buffer-overflow (out-of-bounds read) in memsearch_swar (src/string.c): during substring search the code can invoke memcmp past the end of the target buffer, causing reads beyond the allocated heap. This issue is reachable via mrb_memsearch / mrb_str_index / str_convert_range / mrb_str_aref and can lead to crashes or potential heap memory disclosure.
bug_description.normalized: Stage 01 reproduced an AddressSanitizer `heap-buffer-overflow` with `READ of size 3` in `memsearch_swar` at `src/string.c:647` while executing the staged Ruby source file under `mruby`. The 52-byte witness file is `%w[` followed by 26 bytes of `0xff`, then `r`, then `0xff`, then `].index{|w|w["r   "]}`. mruby parses the `%w[...]` literal into a one-element word array whose haystack string is 28 bytes long and contains a single `'r'` at offset 26, and it also parses the block needle literal `"r   "` into the 4-byte string `72 20 20 20`. `String#[]` with a string index dispatches to `str_index_str()`, which passes `m = 4` and `n = 28` into `mrb_memsearch()` and then `memsearch_swar()`. In the vulnerable fallback loop, `len = e - p` is computed before `memchr(p, *xs, len)` searches for `'r'`; when `memchr()` relocates `p` to `ys + 26`, only 2 bytes remain from `p` to `e`, but the guard still checks the stale `len < m` value from before the relocation. The subsequent `memcmp(p+1, xs+1, m-1)` compares 3 bytes starting from the final haystack byte and reads past the heap allocation. The fix patch makes the missing obligation explicit by changing the guard from `len < m` to `(e - p) < m` after `memchr()` returns.

source.description: First project parser statement that materializes attacker-controlled bytes from the Ruby source file into a string-literal node later executed as the haystack `%w[...]` element.
source.value_from: The staged PoC file `gt_results/secbench_oss_mruby.ossfuzz-42532953/poc` is 52 bytes: ASCII `%w[` + 26 bytes `0xff` + `r` + `0xff` + `].index{|w|w["r   "]}`. This `parse_string()` statement copies the 28-byte word token `ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff 72 ff` into a `NODE_STR` literal.
source.note: This is the scored source rather than `main()` or `mrb_load_detect_file_cxt()` because it is the first project-code statement that turns the attacker-controlled file bytes into the specific string data later searched by the vulnerable substring routine.

relation.description: Source identity relation for the vulnerability-relevant value.

root_cause.description: After `memchr()` may advance `p`, the fallback scan still checks the stale pre-search `len` instead of recomputing the remaining bytes from the new `p` to `e` before allowing the comparison.
root_cause.note: For the witness path, the loop enters this guard with stale `len == 28`, `m == 4`, and `p` newly relocated to `ys + 26`, so the actual remaining span is only `e - p == 2`. The patch changes this exact missing post-`memchr` condition to `(e - p) < m`.

sink.description: Crash site. The fallback substring scan compares `m-1` bytes starting at `p+1` even though the relocated candidate `p` is already too close to `e`, so `memcmp()` reads past the end of the haystack allocation.
sink.note: Stage 01's ASan trace reports `READ of size 3` through `memcmp` with `memsearch_swar /gt/_work/src/src/string.c:647:11` at the top of the project stack, matching `m - 1 == 3` for the 4-byte needle `"r   "`.

tainted_value_origin.description: The parser token buffer is the exact producer of the attacker-controlled literal bytes that become the haystack `%w[...]` element and the later string needle.

parser_admitted.description: The staged input is admitted as Ruby source, not an `.mrb` binary, because the detection gate takes the text-parsing branch.

admitted_location.code: return mrb_load_exec(mrb, mrb_parse_file_continue(mrb, fp, leading.b, bufsize, c), c);

evidence_limitations: Stage 01 reproduced only the vulnerable build. `patch_resolves` remains false here because this Stage 02 role did not execute fixed-build validation.

The parser-to-runtime transition from `NODE_STR` literals to the `RString` operands observed in `mrb_str_aref()` is reconstructed from source and the saved stack, not from additional runtime probes, per the Stage 02 constraints.

fine_trace.note: Source. While parsing the `%w[...]` literal, `parse_string()` copies the 28-byte token `ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff 72 ff` into a `NODE_STR` literal that later becomes the haystack string searched by `w["r   "]`.
The same parser path later materializes the block needle literal `"r   "` as a second `NODE_STR`, preserving the attacker-controlled 4-byte sequence `72 20 20 20` that becomes the substring pattern.

depends_on.via: return mrb_load_exec(mrb, mrb_parse_file_continue(mrb, fp, leading.b, bufsize, c), c);

fine_trace.note: Executing `w["r   "]` reaches the string-index branch of `String#[]`: `indx` is the tainted needle string from step 2, so mruby dispatches to substring search instead of integer or range indexing.
The search helper extracts the needle pointer and length from the string index operand, yielding `ptr = "r   "` and `len = 4`, and forwards them with `offset = 0` into `mrb_str_index()`.

The haystack literal from step 1 has `RSTRING_LEN(str) == 28`, so the pre-search size check passes for `offset = 0` and `slen = 4`. `mrb_str_index()` therefore passes haystack pointer `s`, search size `len = 28`, and needle size `slen = 4` to `mrb_memsearch()`.

Because `mrb_memsearch()` received `m = 4` and `n = 28`, the general SWAR path is chosen. On a 64-bit build, `lim = 28 - 4 - 8 = 16`; after the SWAR loop advances `i` to 16 without returning, the remaining-tail test `i + m < n` still holds (`20 < 28`), so execution falls into the byte-by-byte fallback loop.

Root cause. The fallback scan starts with `p = ys` and `e = ys + 28`, so `len` is computed as 28 before searching for the first needle byte `'r'`. `memchr()` relocates `p` to the witness haystack's only `'r'` at `ys + 26`, which leaves only `e - p == 2` bytes including the matched `'r'`, but the guard still checks stale `len == 28` and therefore fails to break.

Sink. With `p == ys + 26` and `m == 4`, the code requests `memcmp()` of `m - 1 == 3` bytes starting at `p + 1 == ys + 27`, but only the final haystack byte is still in-bounds there. The saved ASan report is therefore a `READ of size 3` from `memcmp` at this line.

format.name: mruby source file
format.contract: The file must be admitted as Ruby source and execute `.index{|w| w["r   "]}` on a `%w[...]` array whose single word is exactly 28 bytes long and ends with `0x72 0xff`, so substring search looks for the 4-byte needle `72 20 20 20` and `memchr()` relocates the candidate `'r'` to within fewer than 4 bytes of the haystack end.
